patches.old: Your tag should be written on your scratch paper (or the digital notepad on the MCAT). Keep it short.
patches.new: Write your tag on the materials the test center provides: the MCAT gives you a laminated **noteboard booklet** (a cover page plus nine graph-lined wet-erase pages) and a fine-point marker. You cannot bring your own paper, and there is no on-screen notepad — the only built-in tools are highlighting and strikethrough. Keep the tag short.
patches.reason: The MCAT provides a wet-erase noteboard booklet and marker; personal scratch paper and a digital notepad are not available.

patches.old: **Week 3-4:** Introduce timing. Aim to complete your map within the first four to five minutes of your ten-minute window. Practice writing tags in two to three words maximum.
patches.new: **Week 3-4:** Introduce timing. Aim to finish reading *and* mapping within the first four minutes or so of your ten-minute window — the writing itself should take well under a minute in total, spread across the paragraphs. Practice writing tags in two to three words maximum.
patches.reason: Resolves a contradiction with question 448, which treats four minutes spent on the map itself as too long.

patches.old: Passage mapping is meant to be a concise, time-efficient tool, typically taking 1-2 minutes, that supports rather than replaces engagement with questions.
patches.new: Passage mapping is meant to be a concise, time-efficient tool that supports rather than replaces engagement with the questions: the tags themselves should take well under a minute of writing spread through the reading, so that reading plus mapping fits in roughly four minutes.
patches.reason: Aligns the explanation with the lesson's own timing guidance and worked example.

visual.title: The three layers of a passage map
visual.alt: A worked example of a passage map in three layers. Layer one, paragraph tags of two to five words: P1 introduces the topic, intuitions widely trusted; P2 is the thesis, intuitions are unreliable and biased; P3 and P4 give evidence from moral dumbfounding and cultural variation; P5 concedes that intuitions are developmentally necessary; P6 concludes they are heuristics, not standards. Layer two, link words between the tags: BUT, AND, HOWEVER, SO. Layer three, a one-sentence main idea with the author's stance plus a tone note. A side panel matches question types to layers: paragraph function to layer one, contrast and why-is-this-here to layer two, main idea, tone and inference to layer three, and detail questions to the tag that tells you which paragraph to open.
visual.caption: The map is a navigation tool: it stores structure, not details.
